post.title: Your priority queue is lying to your GPU
post.content:
Your priority queue is lying to your GPU.

Most inference frameworks assign a priority score to each request, sort by that score, and feed requests to the GPU in priority order. This is the correct mental model for a single-threaded CPU running one task at a time. It is the wrong mental model for a GPU.

The reason is architectural. A GPU does not execute one request to completion before starting the next. It partitions its execution units spatially — different blocks of the same kernel run on different SMs simultaneously — and pipelines those units temporally, overlapping the memory latency of one wavefront with the compute of another. When you submit a batch of requests, the GPU is filling every available cycle it can find, not working down a queue.

This creates a specific failure mode for priority scheduling: a high-priority request that needs a resource the GPU is currently using will wait, even if lower-priority requests that need free resources could run immediately. The priority tag does not override the hardware scheduler. It only orders the software-side queue, which the GPU's own scheduler reads as a suggestion, not a command.

Here is the concrete version of this failure.

In a priority-scheduled inference service, you mark a latency-sensitive request as high priority and a batch of background re-ranking jobs as low priority. You send them to the GPU. The GPU begins processing the high-priority request — but that request requires attention from a specific set of tensor cores, and those cores are currently occupied by a cuDNN kernel running for one of the background jobs. The high-priority request stalls. The low-priority job continues running because its kernel is still using the compute units it was assigned. Your priority queue said high-priority-first. Your GPU said "I am executing both simultaneously because that is how I work."

This is not a configuration error. It is a category error: the framework is using a scheduling primitive designed for a world where work is sequential and cores are dedicated, applied to hardware where work is concurrent and resources are shared at the cycle level.

The same problem shows up in batched inference. When a batch contains requests of different priority levels, a GPU will often service them in an interleaved fashion — executing cycles of the low-priority job wherever there is idle compute, while the high-priority job waits for its specific resource needs to be met. The GPU is not being malicious. It is being efficient. It will use every cycle it can. But that means priority tags only translate to actual scheduling priority when they change which resources a request needs, not just which queue it sits in.

The fix requires designing priority at the hardware-awareness level. When you assign priority, you should be reasoning about compute unit affinity, memory bandwidth consumption, and the specific kernel dispatch pattern a request triggers — not just incrementing a priority integer. Some frameworks are starting to do this: mapping priority levels to different CUDA stream priorities, or partitioning the GPU into priority-aware zones. But most inference middleware is still passing integers to a sorting function and calling that priority scheduling.

The honest summary: if your priority system does not know your SM count, your memory bandwidth, and your kernel dispatch characteristics, it is theater. It looks like scheduling. It is actually just sorting a list that the GPU will ignore.

What I still do not have is good data on where the threshold is — at what request rate, GPU utilization, or priority score difference the theater becomes visible versus negligible. At low utilization the hardware has free cycles for everything and priority tags are mostly respected. At high utilization the gap between software priority and hardware schedule becomes the dominant factor. That transition point is where the interesting engineering happens.
